title: Darshan: the deity looks back
hookLine: the temple curtain opens, and a crowd leans in to see the deity and be seen
carry: darshan: you see the deity, and are seen
tomorrow: How does the Gita say to sit?

lines: A CROWD LEANS IN TO SEE.
WHAT IF THE MARK IS SACRED?
cards: Evening at a temple. A small crowd stands packed in front of a closed curtain, shoes left at the door, hands holding flowers and little plates of sweets. Bells.
Then the curtain is drawn aside, the lamp is lifted, and there is the image of the deity, dressed and garlanded, eyes wide. Nobody in the crowd looks away. Some fold their hands.
A grandfather lifts a small boy higher so he can see. This is darshan. When the thing you gaze at is not a mark on a wall, what changes?

teach.b: Darshan means seeing, or a sight. In temple worship it names the moment of beholding the deity in the image, the murti. People go to the temple for darshan the way they'd go to visit family.

And the teaching underneath is this: for the devotee, God is truly present in the murti, so darshan isn't only looking. As many devotees describe it, the deity is also looking back. The worshipper sees, and is seen.

That's why a murti's eyes are so wide, and why in many temples the eyes of a new image are the last part to be opened, in a rite of their own. The Bhagavad Gita has a scene about the limits of that seeing.

teach.h: ARJUNA IS GIVEN A DIVINE EYE.
teach.b: In chapter eleven, Arjuna asks Krishna to show him his supreme form. And Krishna answers, in paraphrase: you cannot see me with these eyes of yours. I give you a divine eye.
Behold my power. Then the vision comes, vast and blazing, more than Arjuna can hold, and he begs to see the familiar, gentle form again.

teach.h: A FORM YOU CAN LOOK AT.
teach.b: Many teachers read the murti in that light: God, who is more than any eye can hold, takes a form a person can look at, and lets himself be seen.
Some who practice trataka choose a sacred image as their point. The method stays the same: a steady gaze, a gentle return. But the gaze is now attention offered to someone.
Teachers differ: some keep trataka to a flame, others welcome a sacred image.

how: Temple-goers speak of going for darshan, the sight of the deity present in the murti, which in some temples comes at set times when the curtain is opened and a lamp is offered; many devotees describe it as seeing and being seen.

o: a lamp waved before a deity at evening worship
the temple moment when the curtain is drawn aside
a still gaze at a point, which can be a sacred image

s: in darshan, as devotees describe it, only the worshipper does the seeing
some describe it as two-way: the worshipper sees the deity, and is seen.
in the Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna his ordinary eyes can't see the supreme form
in chapter eleven Krishna says so, and gives him a divine eye.
every teacher of trataka uses only a flame or a dot
teachers differ: some keep to a flame or a dot, others welcome a sacred image.

games.q: you're Arjuna. you've asked to see Krishna's supreme form, and he says your eyes can't see it. what happens next?
o: he gives you a divine eye.
he tells you to close your eyes.
games.why: Krishna gives Arjuna a divine eye, and the vast, blazing form appears, more than Arjuna can hold.

practice: If you keep a sacred image, a deity, a symbol, a photo of a teacher, set it at eye level; if not, a flame or a simple mark is just as good.

Rest the eyes on it softly, blinking when you need to, and if it's an image that matters to you, let the gaze feel like a greeting rather than a stare. When the eyes tire, close them and hold what stays, then look again.

wordCard.voice: Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, its neighbor darshan, where the gaze rests on a sacred image, and the worshipper sees and is seen.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: darshana, seeing, a sight. In temple worship, beholding the deity in the murti.

carryVoice: Your line: darshan: you see the deity, and are seen. The image, this time, looks back. Rest well.
